doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

title: Click tracks across changing time signatures
summary: He explains doubling the click to a common denominator, and that 'We Came Through the Storm' was cut without a click.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: The recordings that I’ve heard I was envisioning or wondering if you use a click track ever?
You do. So if it’s – you use changing time signatures but the click can remain constant through those?
Yeah because it depends on what it is. Because if there’s a lot of time signature changes you can find the common denominator and you can change the click track to the common denominator –
So it’s a prepared click track is that correct?

Well not necessarily. Because like for example let’s say we have a song where the tempo is like one-two-three-four, one-two-three-four, and it’s a 4/4 thing, right? And later after that we’re going to do something that’s in 7/8 like a don-don-don, don-don-don, don-don- don, don-don-don. You’re not going to want to use that quarter note click track because the 7/8 part is going to be off. So then it would end up sounding like – I’m going to do a 4/4 part and the 7/8 part. So it’s like one-two-three-four, one-two-three-four, don-don- don, don-don-don, don-don-don, don-don-don – which works. But if you double that click then you can still treat the 4/4 part the same it’s just double the amount of clicks. So you can go one-two-three-four, one-two-three-four, don-don-don, don-don-don, don-don- don, don-don-don. You know? Or – that might not have been the best example but like you can change the – sometimes you can double the amount of clicks that you hear in order for it to fit better over multiple types of time changes.

Sure. Like you get a piece of written music and it says quarter note equals 124 BPMs you could have that be an eighth note instead and go through those time changes I guess. So how do your bandmates –
Well here wait – like here’s an example. So like it’d be like one-two-three-four, one-two- three-four, one-two-three-four-five-six-seven. You see how that one ended up on the off- beat?

If you put that one to end up on a downbeat you just double that. One-two-three-four, one-two-three-four, one-two-three-four-five-six-seven, one-two-three-four-five-six- seven, one-two-three-four-five-six-seven, one-two-three-four, one-two-three, one-two- three, one-two-three, one-two-three, one-two, one-two, one-two-three-four-five-six, one- two-three-four-five-six, one-two-three-four, one-two-three-four, one-two-three-four-five- six-seven, one-two-three-four-five-six-seven, one-two-three-four-five-six, one-two-three- four-five, one-two-three-four, one-two-three, one-two, one. You know like that’s just so to click in to stay, if you find like a common denominator then yeah. But there are times where there are parts where we can’t use the click also. Like there’s a part on a song called “We Came Through the Storm.” And in the studio we played that without a click because there’s a part that like speeds up gradually with the whole band over time and we’re like listening to each other in order for it to speed up. So there’s no click track on that for example.
